items.body:
> **Evidence base:** ANZCOR 11.9; BJA Education antiarrhythmic series (2023); ESC 2024 and ACC/AHA/HRS 2023 AF guidelines, with the APHRS 2026 update. Use the rhythm-specific algorithm and local drug protocol; cardiac-arrest and perfusing-patient regimens differ. [R1–R4]

Review symptoms, baseline ECG, structural disease, QT/pre-excitation, previous treatment and device status. Correct reversible factors, continue indicated established therapy and agree the monitoring/rescue and anticoagulation plan. Defer elective surgery for significant untreated instability; obtain specialist advice when needed. [R1, R3–R4]

## 1.1 Systematic approach to a rhythm disturbance

- Is the patient **haemodynamically unstable**? (hypotension, ischaemia, acute heart failure, reduced consciousness)
- Confirm the rhythm: 12-lead (or monitor strip), check leads and artefact; check pulse and arterial trace.
- Treat reversible causes while preparing definitive therapy.
- Choose therapy by stability and rhythm (below).

Causes of intra-operative arrhythmia

| **Group** | **Bradycardia** | **Tachycardia** |
|---|---|---|
| Anaesthetic and drugs | Opioids (remifentanil), dexmedetomidine, neostigmine, suxamethonium (repeat dose), high spinal | Light anaesthesia, desflurane, ketamine, pancuronium, vasopressors, anticholinergics, LA toxicity |
| Surgical | Vagal stimulation (peritoneal traction, eye muscle, laparoscopic insufflation, carotid), pneumoperitoneum | Pain, bleeding, catecholamine release (phaeochromocytoma), cement, tourniquet |
| Patient | Heart block, sick sinus, raised ICP (Cushing), hypothermia, hypothyroid, beta-blockers | Pre-existing AF, WPW, hyperthyroid, fever, sepsis, anaemia, hypovolaemia |
| Metabolic and physiological | Hypoxia (severe), hypercarbia (later), hypokalaemia/hyperkalaemia | Hypoxia, hypercarbia, hypo/hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, acidosis, MH |
| Mechanical | Central line guidewire, pulmonary artery catheter | Same (ventricular ectopy) |

## 1.2 Unstable arrhythmias

Bradycardia with adverse features

- Atropine 500–600 micrograms IV; repeat every 3–5 min to a total of 3 mg under ANZCOR guidance. Do not delay pacing in high-grade/infranodal block with poor perfusion. In a transplanted heart, avoid atropine: it may be ineffective and provoke AV block. [R1]
- Adrenaline infusion 2–10 microgram/min, isoprenaline, or dopamine if atropine fails.
- Transcutaneous pacing (see section 4) or transvenous pacing if unresponsive; treat cause (stop surgical stimulus, drugs).
- Risk of asystole: recent asystole, Mobitz II, complete heart block (especially broad QRS or very slow escape), or ventricular pauses over 3 s. Seek expert help and prepare pacing even if the immediate drug response is satisfactory. [R1]

Tachycardia with adverse features

- Immediate synchronised DC cardioversion for a tachyarrhythmia causing haemodynamic compromise; confirm synchronisation before each shock.
  - Give sedation/anaesthesia when feasible without delaying treatment.
  - Escalate energy and use rhythm-appropriate drugs if refractory; do not automatically give amiodarone to every rhythm, especially pre-excited AF or torsades. [R1, R3–R4]
- Broad-complex tachycardia: treat as VT unless established otherwise. Pulseless VT/VF and sustained polymorphic VT require unsynchronised defibrillation; a polymorphic rhythm cannot reliably be synchronised. Cardiac arrest follows ALS (Set 9). [R1]
- Torsades de pointes: magnesium sulfate 2 g IV (about 8 mmol; rate adjusted to urgency/local protocol), stop QT-prolonging drugs and correct electrolyte abnormalities.
  - Defibrillate sustained/unstable polymorphic VT, even with a pulse.
  - For recurrent acquired pause-dependent torsades, seek overdrive pacing or specialist-guided isoprenaline; isoprenaline is not routine treatment for congenital long-QT syndrome. [R1, R4]

## 1.3 Stable arrhythmias and drugs

Principles

- Most perioperative arrhythmias need no drug treatment; correct precipitants (hypoxia, hypovolaemia, pain, electrolytes, drugs, light anaesthesia), then clarify the treatment goal (rate control vs rhythm control).
- Antiarrhythmics show **use dependency** (greater effect at fast rates and in depolarised, ischaemic tissue) and can be proarrhythmic at higher doses.
- Isolated PVCs or brief non-sustained VT without compromise usually need assessment and correction of causes rather than suppression.
  - Recurrent, symptomatic, polymorphic or ischaemia-associated episodes need urgent review, structural/ischaemic assessment and rhythm-specific treatment.
  - Magnesium is not a universal treatment for all ventricular ectopy. [R2, R4]

Modified Singh–Vaughan Williams classification

| **Class** | **Examples** | **Use and key points** |
|---|---|---|
| 0: HCN (If) blocker | Ivabradine | Oral sinus-rate reduction in selected heart failure/angina patients; not acute AF rate control. Small perioperative studies do not establish routine intubation prophylaxis. |
| 1a | Procainamide, quinidine | SVT, AF, VT; rarely used (haemodynamic instability, proarrhythmia) |
| 1b | Lidocaine, mexiletine | Ventricular arrhythmia, especially ischaemic; loading/infusion vary by context and local protocol (often 1–1.5 mg/kg, then 1–4 mg/min). Reduce in low output/hepatic dysfunction; CNS toxicity and seizures; not useful for atrial arrhythmias. |
| 1c | Flecainide | Selected AF rhythm control; avoid ischaemic/significant structural disease. Pill-in-pocket requires prior safety assessment; an AV-nodal agent is usually paired to prevent 1:1 flutter, except that pre-excited AF needs its own pathway. |
| 1d | Ranolazine | Late sodium-current inhibition; principally antianginal, with investigated antiarrhythmic roles. Renal/hepatic/QT and interaction restrictions depend on the product information; not routine perioperative AF prevention. |
| 2 | Beta-blockers (esmolol, metoprolol, propranolol), atropine, glycopyrrolate, digoxin, adenosine | Esmolol: titrated loading/infusion (often 0.5 mg/kg then 0.05–0.2 mg/kg/min); avoid haemodynamic collapse. Digoxin loading is divided and adjusted for renal function/age. Adenosine: rapid IV bolus 6 mg then 12 mg per local algorithm for suitable regular SVT; avoid pre-excited AF and significant active bronchospasm. |
| 3 | Amiodarone, sotalol, ibutilide, vernakalant | See below |
| 4 | Verapamil, diltiazem | AV-nodal rate control/AVNRT in suitable patients; titrate slowly to BP and LV function. Avoid pre-excited AF and significant LV systolic dysfunction/decompensated HF. Diltiazem is commonly weight-based (0.25 mg/kg), not one fixed 20 mg dose for everyone. |
| Other | Magnesium | IV magnesium for torsades and documented deficiency. Digoxin toxicity needs specialist/toxicology advice and digoxin-specific Fab when indicated; magnesium is not a substitute for Fab. |

Class 3 points

- Reverse use dependency: IKr blockers (sotalol, ibutilide) prolong the AP most at slow rates, so risk torsades; amiodarone also blocks IKs (normal use dependency) so is less proarrhythmic.
- Amiodarone: cardiac-arrest dosing is 300 mg IV/IO for shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT, with a further 150 mg if indicated by ALS.
  - In perfusing patients, dose and infusion rate depend on the rhythm: do not use an arrest push-dose for stable AF.
  - For AF, ESC 2024 describes 300 mg over 30–60 min followed by 900–1200 mg over 24 h; refractory VT after shocks follows the applicable tachycardia protocol.
  - Titrate the infusion to haemodynamics.
  - Elimination is prolonged and variable (weeks to months).
  - Acute effects include hypotension, bradycardia and myocardial depression; chronic effects include pulmonary, hepatic, thyroid and neurological toxicity.
  - Selected cardiac-surgical prophylaxis reduces AF incidence, but there is no universal 50–65% effect for every regimen.
  - Avoid IV amiodarone in pre-excited AF. [R1–R4]
- Sotalol: renal dosing and QT monitoring are essential; avoid prolonged QT and relevant electrolyte depletion.
  - Ibutilide: 1 mg over 10 min (0.01 mg/kg if under 60 kg), with continuous ECG and post-dose monitoring for torsades.
  - Vernakalant: 3 mg/kg then, if appropriate, 2 mg/kg for selected recent-onset AF; availability and contraindications matter (including hypotension, severe aortic stenosis and advanced heart failure).
  - These are specialist choices, not interchangeable treatments. [R2–R4]

- Stable tachycardia: regular narrow-complex SVT → vagal manoeuvres, then rapid IV adenosine when appropriate; if persistent, seek rhythm-specific treatment.
- Regular broad-complex tachycardia → treat as VT and obtain expert advice, avoiding verapamil/diltiazem for uncertain VT.
- Irregular broad-complex rhythm → consider pre-excited AF or polymorphic VT; do not give reflex adenosine.
- Sinus tachycardia requires treatment of its cause, not routine cardioversion. [R1, R4]

Perioperative AF

- **Preop:** Establish baseline rhythm, symptoms, AF duration, ventricular/valvular disease, prior stroke and anticoagulant indication/last dose.
  - Use a validated thromboembolic-risk framework (e.g. ESC CHA2DS2-VA or the locally adopted score), procedural bleeding risk and a documented anticoagulation plan.
  - Postoperative AF is common, especially after cardiac surgery, but incidence and spontaneous conversion vary by population. [R3–R4]

- **Intraop:** Correct triggers and decide rate versus rhythm control.
  - In stable AF, a titrated beta-blocker may be useful if perfusion permits; diltiazem/verapamil require preserved LV systolic function and should be avoided in decompensated HFrEF.
  - Digoxin may help in selected impaired-LV-function patients but has slower onset and less effect during adrenergic stress.
  - Amiodarone or electrical cardioversion may be appropriate when rhythm control is needed; vernakalant is restricted to selected patients.
  - Do not apply this approach to pre-excited AF. [R2–R4] If AF causes haemodynamic instability, perform immediate synchronised cardioversion.

- **Postop:** Monitor recurrence, treat triggers and assess anticoagulation promptly rather than waiting for 48 h.
  - For non-emergency cardioversion of AF lasting more than 24 h or of uncertain onset, ESC 2024 recommends at least 3 weeks therapeutic anticoagulation or imaging to exclude thrombus; most need at least 4 weeks anticoagulation afterwards, with longer treatment based on stroke risk.
  - Instability requires urgent cardioversion without delaying for imaging/anticoagulation; institute anticoagulation as soon as appropriate, balancing surgical bleeding.
  - Arrange follow-up for trigger-associated AF. [R3–R4]

- Pre-excited AF (typically an irregular broad-complex tachycardia): avoid AV-node-blocking agents, including digoxin, verapamil/diltiazem, beta-blockers, adenosine and IV amiodarone, because VF may result.
- If unstable, cardiovert immediately; if stable, expert-guided IV procainamide or ibutilide are established options where available.
- Distinguish regular narrow-complex orthodromic AVRT: vagal manoeuvres/adenosine may be appropriate under monitored conditions; the AF prohibition is not a blanket ban on adenosine for every patient with an accessory pathway. [R4]

## 1.4 Arrhythmias in postoperative and critical illness

- Common: AF (new-onset in sepsis, post-surgery), VT, SVT, bradycardia; link to electrolytes, catecholamines, sepsis, hypoxia, drugs, central lines.
- Correct hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and calcium/acid–base abnormalities with renal function and repeat levels in mind.
  - High-normal potassium is often targeted for recurrent ventricular arrhythmia/torsades, but K 4–5 mmol/L and Mg above 1.0 mmol/L are not universal requirements for every ICU arrhythmia.
  - Treat infection and reduce avoidable adrenergic triggers. [R1, R4]
- New AF with instability caused by the rhythm: synchronised cardioversion.
  - Stable AF: individualise rate/rhythm control according to ventricular function, perfusion and adrenergic state.
  - Assess AF duration, stroke risk and bleeding from the outset; benefit of anticoagulation during sepsis-associated critical illness is uncertain, so do not impose a blanket 48-h rule.
  - Reassess anticoagulation and recurrence after recovery. [R3–R4]
- QT prolongation: review drugs (ondansetron, haloperidol, macrolides, methadone), keep K and Mg replete.
- Electrical storm (recurrent sustained VT/VF requiring therapy): urgent electrophysiology/critical-care input, defibrillation/cardioversion as appropriate, correction of ischaemia and triggers, analgesia/sedation, tailored antiarrhythmics and sympathetic suppression.
  - Consider device interrogation, ablation, autonomic intervention and mechanical support in refractory cases.
  - Distinguish monomorphic VT from QT-related polymorphic VT before giving amiodarone. [R1, R4]
- Persistent bradycardia with high vagal tone: atropine, chronotropes, pacing; temporary wire for high-grade block.

## 1.5 ANZCOR classification and adverse features

> **Source:** ANZCOR Guideline 11.9, Managing Acute Dysrhythmias (2026). ANZCOR does not give ECG criteria for distinguishing individual rhythms (for example VT versus SVT with aberrancy), so this section covers the guideline's classification only. [R1]

- Give oxygen, obtain IV access and record a 12-lead ECG, without delaying treatment.
- Stable patients without adverse signs usually need no emergency rhythm treatment; seek expert help (for example cardiology) when urgency is low or the choice of treatment is uncertain.
- A pulseless patient with either a bradyarrhythmia or a tachyarrhythmia follows the cardiac arrest algorithm (ANZCOR 11.2; see 1.7 and Set 9).

| Rhythm | Adverse signs that need immediate treatment |
|---|---|
| Bradyarrhythmia | Systolic BP below 90 mmHg; heart rate below 40/min; ventricular arrhythmia; heart failure |
| Tachyarrhythmia | Systolic BP below 90 mmHg; heart rate above 150/min; chest pain; heart failure; drowsiness or confusion |

Classify a stable tachyarrhythmia by QRS width (narrow is normal duration; broad is 0.12 s or longer) and then by regularity:

| QRS and regularity | Rhythms included | ANZCOR approach |
|---|---|---|
| Narrow, regular | Sinus tachycardia, AVNRT, AVRT (WPW), atrial flutter with regular conduction | Vagal manoeuvres first (for example Valsalva). If it persists and is not flutter: adenosine 6 mg rapid IV bolus with a flush of at least 20 mL, then 12 mg if needed (repeatable). If adenosine fails or is contraindicated: verapamil 2.5–5 mg IV over 2 min or diltiazem 15–20 mg over 2 min. |
| Narrow, irregular | Usually AF, sometimes flutter with variable block | Options are rate control, rhythm control (drugs or electrical cardioversion) and prevention of complications (anticoagulation). AF lasting more than 48 h: do not cardiovert (electrical or chemical) until fully anticoagulated, unless transoesophageal echo excludes atrial clot. Acute rate control: IV beta blocker (for example metoprolol 5 mg IV) or digoxin 250–500 microgram IV or oral; beta blockers are contraindicated with bronchospasm or decompensated heart failure. Avoid AV-nodal blockers and digoxin in pre-excitation. |
| Broad, regular | Presume VT (peri-arrest) | Amiodarone 300 mg IV over 20–60 min, then 900 mg over 24 h. Monitor, seek expert help, and be ready to cardiovert if adverse signs develop or the rhythm persists for hours. IV lignocaine for stable VT associated with ischaemia or infarction. Avoid verapamil and diltiazem in broad-complex tachycardia of unknown origin, especially with myocardial dysfunction. |
| Broad, irregular | Most likely AF with bundle branch block; consider pre-excited AF or polymorphic VT such as torsades | Seek expert help. In suspected pre-excited AF or flutter, avoid adenosine, digoxin, verapamil and diltiazem; electrical cardioversion is usually safest. For torsades, see 1.8. |

## 1.6 Cardioversion, defibrillation and pacing practicalities

> **Source:** ANZCOR Guidelines 11.9 (2026) and 11.4, Electrical Therapy for Adult Advanced Life Support (page lists approval July 2025). ANZCOR 11.9 and 11.4 do not give synchronised cardioversion energy levels or sedation agents and doses, so none are stated here; use the device manufacturer's guidance and your local protocol. [R1, R18]

**Tachycardia with adverse features caused by the arrhythmia**

- Immediate synchronised cardioversion, with sedation as required.
- If cardioversion fails: amiodarone 300 mg IV over 10–20 min, repeat cardioversion, then an infusion of 900 mg over 24 h.

**Defibrillation (unsynchronised) energy**

- Biphasic: the default energy is 200 J for all shocks.
- Monophasic: set the maximum energy (usually 360 J) for all shocks.
- If the first shock fails and the device can deliver more, it is reasonable to increase to the maximum available for subsequent shocks.

**Pad position**

- Standard (anterolateral): one pad to the right of the upper sternum below the clavicle; the other (apical) in the mid-axillary line, clear of breast tissue.
- Large breasts: place the left pad lateral to or underneath the left breast, avoiding breast tissue.
- Alternatives are anterior–posterior, bi-axillary and postero-lateral (one pad in the left mid-axillary line, the other on the back just below the right scapula).
- Self-adhesive pads are preferred over paddles, and they make pacing possible.
- Pacemaker or ICD in place: pad placement should not delay defibrillation; place pads ideally at least 8 cm from the generator; alternative positions are acceptable.

**Safety**

- Warn of the impending discharge with a "stand clear" command.
- Do not continue chest compressions during the shock.
- Avoid placing pads over ECG electrodes, medication patches, implanted devices or central line sites.
- Avoid shocking in an oxygen-enriched atmosphere (for example high-flow oxygen across the chest).
- Avoid contact with the patient and with metal fixtures such as bed rails.
- If a shock does not appear to have been delivered, consider that synchronise mode may be on.

**External pacing (ANZCOR 11.9)**

- Indicated when drugs fail or the patient is at high risk of asystole (recent asystole, Mobitz II, complete heart block with a broad QRS or rate below 40/min, or ventricular standstill over 3 s).
- Demand mode at 70–80/min, starting around 30 mA and increasing until capture; asynchronous mode may be used pre-hospital.
- Skeletal muscle stimulation can cause discomfort.

## 1.7 Cardiac arrest rhythms: ANZCOR recap

> **Source:** ANZCOR Guidelines 11.2 (approved June 2024), 11.4 and 11.5 (approved April 2025). This is a recap for rhythm questions; the full arrest protocol is in Set 9 and ANZCOR 11.2. Cardiac arrest from trauma and post-cardiac-surgery arrest are not covered here. [R1, R17–R19]

**Shockable (VF or pulseless VT)**

- Shock, resume chest compressions immediately, and continue 2 minutes of CPR after each shock; pause about every 2 minutes for rhythm analysis.
- Charge a manual defibrillator during CPR as the 2-minute loop nears its end.
- Escalation: defibrillate and ensure good CPR; defibrillate then add adrenaline 1 mg (after the 2nd shock); defibrillate then add amiodarone 300 mg (after the 3rd shock).
- Repeat adrenaline every second loop (about every 4 minutes).
- An additional amiodarone 150 mg may be considered after the 5th shock; an infusion of 15 mg/kg over 24 h may be considered after recurrent VF or pulseless VT.
- Lignocaine is an alternative to amiodarone: 1 mg/kg, a further 0.5 mg/kg after the 5th shock, and an infusion of 1–4 mg/min after recurrent VF or pulseless VT.
- Avoid amiodarone in torsades.

**Non-shockable (PEA or asystole)**

- Defibrillation is not indicated; focus on CPR, IV or IO access, airway, drugs, pacing and correcting reversible causes.
- Give adrenaline 1 mg as soon as feasible during CPR, then every second loop.

**During CPR**

- Reversible causes. 4 Hs: hypoxaemia, hypovolaemia, hyper/hypokalaemia and metabolic disorders, hypo/hyperthermia. 4 Ts: tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins/poisons/drugs, thrombosis (pulmonary or coronary).
- If hypovolaemia is suspected, give at least 20 mL/kg crystalloid.
- Give 100% oxygen when available. Consider a supraglottic airway or tracheal tube, but airway attempts should not interrupt CPR for more than 5 seconds.
- Waveform capnography is recommended to confirm airway placement and monitor CPR quality.
- IV access is preferred over IO; use IO if IV attempts fail or are not feasible.
- Routine calcium, sodium bicarbonate and magnesium are not recommended in arrest. Magnesium is considered for torsades, digoxin toxicity, or documented hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia (5 mmol bolus, repeatable once, then 20 mmol over 2–4 h). Calcium and bicarbonate have specific indications, listed in 1.8.

## 1.8 Cause-specific treatment: ANZCOR

> **Source:** ANZCOR Guidelines 11.9 (2026), 11.10, Resuscitation in Special Circumstances (approved July 2026) and 11.5 (April 2025). Where ANZCOR gives no dose, none is stated. Malignant hyperthermia and dantrolene are not covered by these guidelines, and perioperative anaphylaxis is referred to the ANZCA/ANZAAG guidelines. [R1, R19, R20]

| Cause | ANZCOR treatment |
|---|---|
| Hyperkalaemia | Confirm with a blood gas analyser if available. Calcium chloride 10% 10 mL (or calcium gluconate 30 mL) by rapid IV bolus, repeated if arrest is prolonged or refractory. Short-acting insulin 10 units with glucose 25 g (50 mL of 50%) IV, and monitor blood glucose. Sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol (50 mL of 8.4%) IV for severe acidosis or renal failure; do not mix with calcium chloride. Consider dialysis for hyperkalaemic arrest resistant to medical treatment. |
| Local anaesthetic toxicity | In addition to standard resuscitation, for cardiovascular collapse or arrest: 20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg bolus, then an infusion of 15 mL/kg/h; up to three bolus doses at 5-minute intervals; continue the infusion until stable or up to a total of 12 mL/kg. |
| Beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker toxicity | Consider IV glucagon or insulin/glucose/potassium (11.9). Vasopressors, inotropes, calcium, glucagon, phosphodiesterase inhibitors and high-dose insulin–glucose–potassium infusions may help; high-dose isoprenaline may help refractory beta-blocker bradycardia; pacing may be effective (11.10). No doses are given for most of these. |
| Digoxin toxicity | Heart block and ventricular arrhythmias may be treated with digoxin-specific antibody fragments (no dose given). Magnesium may be considered (11.5). |
| Tricyclic overdose | Sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 1–2 mL/kg (up to 100 mL) IV every 3–5 min, titrated to narrowing of the QRS and a pH of 7.45–7.55; maximum 6 mL/kg total, with expert advice. Alternatively, or additionally, hyperventilate an intubated patient to a PaCO2 of 30–35 mmHg. |
| Torsades de pointes | Stop QT-prolonging drugs, correct electrolytes (especially potassium) and treat causes such as ischaemia. Magnesium 5 mmol IV over 10 min, repeatable once, then 20 mmol over 4 h (11.9; 11.5 states an infusion over 2–4 h). Pace if there is heart block with symptomatic bradycardia. Avoid amiodarone. |
| Hypothermia | Withhold adrenaline if core temperature is below 30 °C; at 30–34 °C lengthen the adrenaline interval to 6–10 min. If VF persists after three shocks, delay further attempts until core temperature is above 30 °C. Rewarm with ECLS where available (ECMO preferred over cardiopulmonary bypass). |
| Anaphylaxis | IM adrenaline early in the anterolateral thigh, repeated after 5 min or sooner if problems persist. Refractory: IV adrenaline infusion; experienced clinicians may consider IV boluses of 10–20 microgram (doubling if unresponsive) while infusions are prepared. In arrest: follow ALS, intubate early if expertise is available, give large IV fluid volumes, and consider additional vasopressors and ECPR. |
| Electrolyte disorders | Life-threatening arrhythmias are most commonly associated with potassium disorders, particularly hyperkalaemia, and less often calcium or magnesium disorders. Treat life-threatening abnormalities before arrest occurs. |

> **Dose check:** the magnesium dose for torsades in section 1.2 (2 g, about 8 mmol) differs from the ANZCOR dose above (5 mmol over 10 min, repeatable once, then 20 mmol). Use the ANZCOR/local protocol dose.

items.los: SS_CS 1.4 (cardiac rhythm, right ventricular function and pulmonary artery pressure, and shunts components)
items.body:
> **Evidence base:** BJA Education RV physiology (2018), ASE right-heart guidance (2025), BJA Education adult congenital heart disease (2025) and current PH guidance. Historical single echo cut-offs and categorical claims about shunts have been updated. [R5–R8]

## 2.1 Cardiac rhythm assessment

| **Question** | **Why it matters** |
|---|---|
| Which rhythm: sinus, AF, flutter, paced, heart block? | Rate control, anticoagulation, device and monitoring plan |
| Symptoms: syncope, palpitations, presyncope | High-grade block, VT, sick sinus |
| 12-lead ECG | PR, QRS, QTc, bundle branch block, pre-excitation, Brugada pattern, ischaemia |
| Drugs | Antiarrhythmics/rate drugs, toxicity and interactions; anticoagulant indication, stroke/bleeding risk and interruption/resumption plan |
| Electrolytes | K, Mg, Ca; QT-prolonging drugs |
| Device | Device type, dependence, battery, alerts, recent interrogation/remote data and planned EMI exposure; timing individualised with device team |
| Echo | Structural disease with VT risk (cardiomyopathy, EF 35% or less) |

**Red flags needing review before elective surgery:** new or uncontrolled arrhythmia, symptomatic bradycardia, high-grade AV block without pacing, VT, long QT with symptoms, rapid AF.

## 2.2 RV function and PA pressure

Normal RV vs LV

|  | **RV** | **LV** |
|---|---|---|
| Shape and wall | Crescent; free wall 1–5 mm; about one sixth of LV muscle mass | Ellipsoid; 8–10 mm |
| Pressures | Systolic 15–30, diastolic 0–8 mmHg | Systolic 90–140, diastolic 4–12 mmHg |
| Afterload | Normal PVR approximately 0.5–2 WU (40–160 dyn·s·cm⁻⁵); much lower than systemic resistance | SVR 800–1200 |
| Perfusion | Normally throughout the cycle; higher RV pressure/wall stress reduces systolic flow, increasing reliance on diastolic perfusion | Mainly diastole |
| Tolerance | Relatively compliant in health; failing/dilated RV is vulnerable to fluid overload and very sensitive to acute afterload increase | Thicker wall supports systemic pressure; both ventricles can fail with excessive preload or afterload |
| Stroke work | About a quarter of LV |  |

- PVR = (mean PAP − PAWP) / CO in Wood units; multiply by 80 for dyn·s·cm⁻⁵. Normal resting PVR is approximately 0.5–2 WU; PVR is only part of RV afterload, which also includes pulmonary arterial compliance and wave reflection. [R5–R7]
- **Ventricular interdependence:** RV overload shifts the septum towards the LV (D-shaped LV), reducing LV filling and compliance; the LV may look small and well contracting ("empty") yet the cause is RV failure.
- Positive-pressure ventilation can reduce venous return and increase RV afterload, especially with overdistension; atelectasis and hypoxia also raise PVR. Choose PEEP and tidal volume to balance recruitment against overdistension. Marked SVV/PPV in RV dysfunction does not by itself establish that fluid will help. [R5, R9]

Assessment tools

| **Tool** | **Findings** |
|---|---|
| Clinical | Raised JVP, Kussmaul's sign (RV infarct, constriction), peripheral oedema, loud P2, RV heave |
| CVP | Trends support interpretation of congestion/haemodynamics; neither one CVP nor its rise alone establishes fluid need or treatment failure. TR may produce large v waves; PH may produce prominent a waves. |
| Bloods | BNP, troponin, lactate, renal and liver function for hypoperfusion and congestion |
| ECG | Right-axis deviation, RBBB/RV strain may support a diagnosis; S1Q3T3 is neither sensitive nor specific for PE |
| CXR | CXR may show right-heart/pulmonary-artery enlargement or lung disease but is insensitive and does not quantify RV function or diagnose PH alone. |
| TTE (mainstay) | See below |
| TOE | Better images in ventilated patients and cardiac surgery; consider for high-risk surgery |
| PAC | RHC confirms/classifies PH. A PAC in selected acute RV failure can measure RAP/PAP, PAWP, CO and SvO2; low output with disproportionate RAP may support RV failure, but no single RAP:PAWP or SvO2 cut-off diagnoses it. |

TTE parameters

| **Measure** | **Abnormal** |
|---|---|
| RV size (apical 4-chamber) | Use RV-focused apical four-chamber and indexed context. ASE 2025 basal diameter: normal <41 mm; mild 41–44, moderate >44–49, severe >49 mm. Avoid a simple RV:LV ratio as a complete grading system. [R5] |
| TAPSE | ≤17 mm is abnormal in ASE 2025; load, angle and postoperative longitudinal-motion changes limit isolated interpretation |
| Fractional area change | ≤35% is abnormal in ASE 2025; combine with other RV function measures |
| RVSP | 4 × peak TR velocity² + estimated RAP. Equals PASP only without RVOT/pulmonary obstruction; inaccurate jets/RAP or severe TR can mislead. Echo estimates probability, not definitive PH diagnosis. |
| RA pressure from IVC | Spontaneously breathing adult: IVC ≤21 mm with >50% sniff collapse suggests RAP about 3 mmHg; >21 mm with <50% collapse about 15; discordant findings often about 8 after other signs. Do not apply mechanically to positive-pressure ventilation. [R5] |
| Septal position | Predominant end-diastolic flattening supports volume load; systolic flattening supports pressure load; severe pressure load may flatten both phases. Integrate TR, function and haemodynamics. |

## 2.3 Shunts

Anatomy and direction

- Left-to-right (ASD, VSD, PDA, AVSD): pulmonary overcirculation, lesion-dependent RV/LV volume loading and possible PH.
  - Excessive SVR increase or PVR reduction may increase left-to-right flow; systemic vasodilation generally reduces that gradient, although hypotension still compromises perfusion.
  - If PVR rises sufficiently, flow may reverse.
  - Do not assume every shunt tolerates induction well. [R8]
- Right-to-left (e.g. unrepaired tetralogy or Eisenmenger; a PFO may shunt right-to-left with raised right-sided pressure): hypoxaemia and paradoxical embolism.
  - Substantial right-to-left flow slows inhalational induction and can accelerate IV drug delivery; the actual effect depends on shunt magnitude, mixing and output.
  - Secondary erythrocytosis may coexist with iron deficiency. [R8]
- **Eisenmenger syndrome:** shunt reversal due to fixed high PVR; high perioperative mortality; avoid hypovolaemia and falls in SVR; maintain preload and contractility; avoid factors raising PVR (hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, pain, hypothermia).

### Assessment

- History: cyanosis, exercise tolerance, syncope, haemoptysis, prior endocarditis, paradoxical embolic events.
- Examination: saturation (pre- and post-ductal), clubbing, murmurs, signs of RV failure.
- Investigations: ECG, echo with bubble contrast or colour Doppler (Qp:Qs, direction, PA pressure), haemoglobin and haematocrit (polycythaemia, iron deficiency), coagulation, MRI/catheter data if needed.
- Preop plan: establish repaired/palliated anatomy, residual shunt and ventricular function with congenital-cardiology input; assess thrombosis/bleeding and iron status.
  - Endocarditis prophylaxis depends on both lesion and procedure: a high-risk lesion alone does not require extra antibiotics for every operation.
  - Use the applicable NZ/local prophylaxis guidance. [R8, R10]

**Intraoperative:** Maintain lesion-specific haemodynamics, meticulously de-air IV systems and use suitable air-eliminating filters when indicated without compromising required flow.

**Postoperative:** Monitor oxygenation, rhythm, perfusion and fluid balance; plan analgesia, thromboprophylaxis/anticoagulation and specialist/HDU care according to complexity. [R8]

items.title: 3. Pulmonary hypertension and RV failure: anaesthetic implications
items.los: BT_PO 1.5 (pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure components)
items.body:
> **Evidence base:** ESC/ERS 2022 definitions and treatment principles, the ERS 2026 PAH update, AHA 2023 perioperative PH statement and contemporary perioperative RV consensus. The older BJA Education PH review is retained as background, not authority for current thresholds, routine anticoagulation or universal prognostic percentages. [R6–R7, R9, R11]

## 3.1 Definition, classification and diagnosis

- PH is mean PAP >20 mmHg at rest on right-heart catheterisation.
  - Pre-capillary PH: PAWP ≤15 mmHg and PVR >2 WU; post-capillary PH: PAWP >15 mmHg, with PVR ≤2 WU (isolated) or >2 WU (combined).
  - PAH is group 1 disease meeting pre-capillary criteria after excluding alternative causes.
  - Lower diagnostic thresholds do not automatically establish benefit from PAH drugs in every borderline case. [R6–R7]

| **Group** | **Cause** | **Notes** |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pulmonary arterial hypertension (idiopathic, heritable, connective tissue disease, congenital heart disease, HIV, portal hypertension, drugs) | Pre-capillary; specific therapy |
| 2 | Left heart disease (PCWP above 15 mmHg) | Commonest group overall |
| 3 | Lung disease or hypoxia (COPD, ILD) | Severity varies; severe disease can occur and needs specialist assessment. PAH drugs are not routine for all group 3 PH. |
| 4 | Chronic thromboembolic PH (CTEPH) | Potentially treatable with PEA if operable; BPA and/or medical therapy for selected inoperable/residual disease. Risk/outcomes depend on centre and patient; not all cases are curable. |
| 5 | Miscellaneous (sarcoid, myeloproliferative) |  |

- Symptoms: exertional dyspnoea, then oedema and presyncope; signs: raised JVP, loud P2, RV heave.
- ECG may show right-axis deviation, RV strain or hypertrophy, but a normal ECG does not exclude PH. Echo estimates PH probability from TR velocity plus RV/RA, septal and pulmonary-artery signs; neither sPAP 36 mmHg nor one RVSP estimate diagnoses PH. Assess left-heart disease using the full study. [R5–R7]
- A V/Q scan is recommended to screen for CTEPH in unexplained/newly diagnosed PH; CTPA defines vascular anatomy and other disease, but a negative routine CTPA does not reliably exclude distal CTEPH. RHC confirms/classifies PH when clinically indicated, ideally through a PH centre. [R6–R7]
- Acute vasoreactivity testing is for selected idiopathic, heritable or drug-associated PAH to identify potential high-dose calcium-channel-blocker responders.
  - A positive response is a fall in mPAP ≥10 mmHg to ≤40 mmHg with unchanged/increased CO.
  - Only a minority qualify, and sustained response requires follow-up.
  - It is not routine testing or justification for CCBs in all PH groups. [R6]

## 3.2 Chronic therapy

| **Pathway** | **Drugs** | **Anaesthetic points** |
|---|---|---|
| Prostanoid | Epoprostenol (half-life under 10 min), iloprost, treprostinil | **Never interrupt infusions** (rebound PH, collapse); line infection risk; hypotension, flushing |
| Endothelin antagonist | Bosentan, ambrisentan, macitentan | Oral; bosentan liver derangement |
| NO pathway | Sildenafil, tadalafil, riociguat | PDE5 inhibitors and riociguat must NOT be combined; avoid nitrates with either. Continue established therapy using an agreed perioperative plan. |
| Other | Diuretics; anticoagulation when indicated | CTEPH usually needs lifelong therapeutic anticoagulation; PAH anticoagulation is individualised, not routine for all idiopathic PAH. |
| Activin signalling | Sotatercept | Add-on chronic PAH therapy in selected patients; monitor Hb, platelets, BP and bleeding; not acute rescue therapy. [R11] |

- PAH treatment is risk-based and specialist-directed: many low/intermediate-risk patients without major cardiopulmonary comorbidity start ERA plus PDE5 inhibition; high-risk disease usually requires combination therapy including IV/SC prostacyclin and transplant assessment.
  - Therapy differs for comorbid patients and other PH groups.
  - Sotatercept is an additional pathway option in selected PAH patients already on treatment; ERS 2026 recommends add-on use at intermediate-low, intermediate-high or high follow-up risk.
  - It does not replace a prostacyclin infusion or treat an acute PH crisis. [R6, R11]

- Sotatercept safety: assess haemoglobin, platelets and bleeding history, and monitor blood pressure.
- Erythrocytosis, thrombocytopenia, telangiectasia and serious bleeding matter perioperatively, especially with prostacyclin or antithrombotic therapy.
- Prescribing/withholding decisions belong with the PH centre; this is chronic disease therapy, not rescue vasodilation. [R11; prescribing information]

## 3.3 RV failure physiology

- Vicious cycle: raised PVR → RV dilatation → TR and septal shift → reduced LV filling/output → hypotension → reduced RV coronary perfusion → ischaemia → worse RV failure. Systolic RV coronary flow falls as RV pressure/wall stress increase, making adequate systemic and diastolic perfusion especially important. [R5, R9]
- Precipitants: atrial/ventricular arrhythmia, sepsis (including prostanoid-line infection), anaemia, PE, pericardial disease, metabolic disturbance, drug interruption and volume overload. Loss of sinus rhythm/AV synchrony may be poorly tolerated; do not apply one fixed flutter prevalence to all pre-capillary PH. [R9]
- Factors raising RV afterload/PVR include hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, pain, hypothermia, atelectasis and overdistension/high airway pressure; avoid nitrous oxide.
  - Drug effects depend on dose, ventilation and underlying physiology.
  - Avoid abrupt vasodilation or adrenergic surges; ketamine is not a universal prohibition, but severe PH requires an individual induction plan with expert input. [R9]

## 3.4 Perioperative implications (BT_PO 1.5)

### Preop

- Identify type, severity (WHO class, 6-minute walk, echo TAPSE and RVSP, BNP, right atrial pressure, cardiac index) and current therapy; involve the PH centre and plan ICU/HDU.
- Higher risk includes emergency or major/prolonged surgery, poor functional capacity, RV dysfunction, raised RAP, low CI and clinical decompensation. A requirement for vasoactive support is a marker of illness, not an independent preoperative score applicable to every patient. [R6, R9]
- Risk is strongly population- and procedure-dependent.
  - Ramakrishna’s historical 145-patient cohort reported 7% early mortality; the PAH registry cited by ESC/ERS reported about 2% elective versus 15% emergency mortality.
  - These are different cohorts, not a universal 3.5–7% consent estimate.
  - Explain individual risk with the PH team. [R6; trial table]
- Continue established PH therapies, especially uninterrupted prostacyclin delivery.
  - Plan a dedicated line, trained staff, spare pump/drug and backup power; never flush a prostacyclin line or change delivery casually.
  - If the oral route is unavailable, agree a drug-specific alternative with the PH centre/pharmacy; not every oral agent has an equivalent IV or suitable NG preparation. [R9]
- Optimise volume status, treat infection, arrhythmia and anaemia; avoid prolonged fasting and dehydration.
- Premedication: avoid anxiety and hypoxia but beware oversedation and hypercarbia.

### Intraop

- Aim: maintain RV preload (avoid hypovolaemia and overload), contractility, systemic pressure and sinus rhythm; keep PVR low.
- Monitoring matched to RV disease and surgical risk: arterial pressure monitoring (often before induction in severe disease), reliable access and, where useful, CVP trends, echo and flow monitoring.
  - A PAC may help selected severe/complex cases; benefits depend on the question and expertise, balanced against arrhythmia, infection and PA injury.
  - No single monitor is mandatory or proven to improve outcomes in all PH surgery. [R9]
- Choose general, regional or combined anaesthesia according to lesion, procedure, anticoagulation and expertise.
  - Regional techniques can reduce pain/opioids but abrupt neuraxial sympathectomy may cause collapse; avoid large rapid spinal doses in severe PH and consider carefully titrated techniques.
  - Sedation also risks hypoventilation and airway obstruction. [R9]
- General anaesthesia: prepare vasoactives and rescue pulmonary vasodilators before induction in severe disease.
  - Titrate induction to avoid hypotension and sympathetic surges; drug selection depends on RV reserve.
  - Maintain oxygenation and appropriate CO2/pH, use lung-protective tidal volumes and enough PEEP for recruitment without overdistension, and avoid nitrous oxide.
  - Plan extubation carefully. [R9]
- Norepinephrine or low-dose vasopressin are commonly favoured for hypotension with RV failure.
  - Vasopressin is relatively pulmonary-sparing at usual low doses, not a guaranteed pulmonary vasodilator; high doses can be harmful.
  - Phenylephrine can raise PVR and cause bradycardia, so is usually less attractive in acute RV failure.
  - Titrate to perfusion and output rather than pressure alone. [R9]
- Inotropes/inodilators: dobutamine or milrinone for low output with impaired RV contractility; both can cause systemic hypotension and arrhythmia, and may require a vasopressor. Levosimendan/inhaled milrinone are selected specialist options with less established routine perioperative evidence. [R9]
- Inhaled nitric oxide or inhaled prostacyclin may provide selective short-term RV afterload reduction in a crisis.
  - Ensure a reliable delivery system, monitor systemic pressure and relevant toxicities, and avoid abrupt withdrawal.
  - PAH therapy can worsen pulmonary oedema in pulmonary venous/left-heart disease; identify the PH mechanism first. [R9]
- Treat arrhythmias early; cardioversion if unstable (loss of atrial kick tolerates poorly).

PH/RV crisis: call for help and halt the precipitant if possible; increase oxygen, check airway/ventilation and pH, restore systemic perfusion with titrated vasoactives, assess the RV with echo and avoid reflex large-volume loading. Use inhaled pulmonary vasodilator/inotrope as indicated and escalate early for specialist mechanical support. [R9]

### Postop

- Plan recovery level and duration from PH/RV severity, surgery, analgesia and intraoperative events.
  - Significant PH, RV dysfunction or major surgery often warrants HDU/ICU surveillance through the early postoperative risk period (commonly 24–72 h); this is not a mandatory interval for every patient.
  - Pregnancy/postpartum PH needs a separate specialist plan, with risk extending beyond 72 h. [R6, R9]
- Prevent hypoxia, hypercarbia, pain, shivering; multimodal analgesia with minimal respiratory depression; early return to oral PH therapy.
- Watch for congestion, arrhythmia and RV failure during fluid redistribution. Assess perfusion and volume tolerance with clinical findings, balance/weight, renal function and echo as appropriate; diurese harmful congestion when perfusion permits. A rising CVP alone is not an automatic indication for diuresis. [R9]
- Pulmonary embolism prophylaxis; anticoagulation plans per indication.

## 3.5 Critical care management of acute PH and RV failure

- **Treat the precipitant:** sepsis (including catheter-related infection in prostanoid patients), arrhythmia (restore sinus rhythm, amiodarone or DC cardioversion), anaemia, PE, effusion.
- Optimise RV preload: assess congestion and perfusion together.
  - Diurese the overloaded/dilated RV with monitored loop diuretics, adding other agents as appropriate; consider renal replacement for refractory overload/other indications.
  - If genuinely underfilled, use small reassessed aliquots rather than indiscriminate fluid avoidance or loading. [R9]
- Reduce RV afterload: treat the cause (including reperfusion for high-risk acute PE when indicated); use selective inhaled pulmonary vasodilators as rescue where appropriate.
  - De novo or escalating PAH therapy, including IV prostacyclin, requires the PH centre.
  - Do not empirically apply a PAH regimen to group 2 PH, and do not combine sildenafil/tadalafil with riociguat. [R6, R9]
- Support contractility and systemic perfusion with titrated dobutamine/milrinone and norepinephrine ± low-dose vasopressin as indicated.
  - Maintain adequate aortic–RV coronary perfusion and end-organ flow.
  - “SBP above PA pressure” is a useful physiological concern in severe PH, not a sufficient or universally attainable resuscitation target.
  - Follow lactate, urine output, echo and output as well as pressure. [R9]
- Escalate early for mechanical support/transplant evaluation if recovery or definitive therapy is plausible: VA-ECMO may bridge to treatment, recovery or transplantation in selected patients.
  - Other RV/unloading configurations require specialist selection.
  - CTEPH treatment may include planned pulmonary endarterectomy, balloon pulmonary angioplasty and/or medical therapy; it is not universally an emergency PEA indication. [R6, R9]
- Ventilation is high risk in severe RV failure but must not be withheld when required.
  - Avoid delayed emergency intubation: use expert airway management with pre-induction haemodynamic support, and carefully balance NIV/PEEP benefits against impaired RV filling/afterload.
  - Use renal replacement for appropriate indications, including refractory harmful overload, with cautious fluid removal. [R9]
- Limits of care depend on context (end-stage disease without transplant may be ward-based).
- Prognosis depends on PH cause, RV reserve, precipitant, organ dysfunction and available definitive therapy. Historical ICU mortality percentages from selected older series should not be used as current universal estimates or futility thresholds. Discuss trajectory and goals with PH/critical-care specialists. [R9]

RV dysfunction in ARDS or after cardiac surgery

- In ARDS and after cardiac surgery, selective pulmonary vasodilators may improve haemodynamics/oxygenation transiently without established routine survival benefit.
  - Reduce injurious driving/plateau pressures, recruit without overdistension and treat the cause.
  - RV response is patient-specific and should be reassessed with haemodynamics and echo. [R9]
- Hypoxia, hypercapnia and atelectasis raise PVR; high lung volumes impair RV return.

items.title: 4. Conduction abnormalities, pacemakers and ICDs
items.los: IT_PO 1.4 (cardiac conduction abnormalities and pacemakers component); SS_CS 1.10; SS_CS 1.11; SS_CS 1.12; SS_CS 1.8; BT_RT 1.37
items.body:
> **Evidence base:** Miller’s Anesthesia 10th edition, chapter 34 (directly reviewed); AHA CIED statement 2024; BJA Education temporary epicardial pacing 2023; current resuscitation and MRI/device guidance. The 2016 BJAEd review remains background rather than the sole current device reference. [R1, R12–R15]

## 4.1 Conduction abnormalities and anaesthesia

| **Abnormality** | **Significance** |
|---|---|
| First-degree AV block | Usually benign; avoid drugs that prolong PR if advanced disease |
| Mobitz I (Wenckebach) | Usually nodal, benign; rarely needs pacing |
| Mobitz II, third-degree block | Acquired Mobitz II/high-grade/complete block without reversible cause: specialist pacing assessment, even if asymptomatic; temporary strategy if urgent surgery. [R16] |
| Right bundle branch block | Usually benign in isolation; catheter-induced RIGHT bundle injury is the main concern in pre-existing LBBB, when complete block may occur |
| Left bundle branch block | Assess underlying disease; RV guidewire/PAC manipulation can injure the right bundle and cause complete block when LBBB already exists |
| Bifascicular block (RBBB plus left anterior or posterior hemiblock) | Low risk of progression to complete block intra-operatively; without symptoms no pacing needed |
| Bifascicular block with PR prolongation or syncope | PR prolongation does not prove disease in all three fascicles. Syncope/alternating BBB needs specialist assessment; asymptomatic ECG pattern alone is not an automatic temporary-pacing indication. |
| Sick sinus syndrome | Brady-tachy; sensitive to vagal drugs |

### Preop

- Symptoms (syncope, presyncope), ECG, echo for structural disease, electrolytes, drug review (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, amiodarone, clonidine, dexmedetomidine).
- Acquired Mobitz II, high-grade or third-degree AV block without a reversible/physiological cause warrants cardiology review for permanent pacing even without symptoms; do not restrict this to symptomatic patients. For urgent surgery, arrange an expert temporary-pacing strategy when needed. [R16]
- Consider external pads and capability to pace.

### Intraop

- Anticipate bradycardia with spinal/epidural high block, opioids, suxamethonium, neostigmine, vagal stimuli; have atropine, glycopyrrolate, adrenaline, isoprenaline and pacing ready.
- Avoid agents that depress conduction in advanced block; maintain K, Mg; ECG monitoring with pacing-capable lead.
- Central line and PA catheter placement can induce block in LBBB.

### Postop

- Continuous ECG monitoring; recheck electrolytes; continue or restart rate-affecting drugs carefully; device check if pacing implanted.

## 4.2 Types of cardiac pacing

| **Type** | **Route** | **Typical use** | **Notes** |
|---|---|---|---|
| External (transcutaneous) | Large adhesive pads, anterior–posterior | Emergency bridge; prophylactic pads for high-risk blocks | Sedation/analgesia if perfusion permits. Electrical capture must be matched by a pulse/arterial waveform; output is patient- and device-dependent. |
| Transvenous (temporary) | Balloon-tipped lead via internal jugular, subclavian or femoral vein to RV apex | Symptomatic bradycardia, block after MI, overdrive pacing, cardiac surgery | Risks: perforation, tamponade, infection, arrhythmia; threshold and sensing checks daily |
| Epicardial | Wires sewn to atrium/ventricle at cardiac surgery, exiting through skin | Post-cardiac-surgery bradycardia and block | Threshold rises over days; remove carefully (bleeding, tamponade risk) |
| Permanent (endocardial) | Pulse generator under left clavicle with leads in RA/RV (and coronary sinus for CRT) | Chronic block, sick sinus, heart failure with wide QRS (CRT) | See 4.3 |
| Leadless | Intracardiac capsule(s), typically RV; newer systems may include an RA unit | Selected bradycardia/AV-synchrony indications | Avoids transvenous leads/pocket but has implantation/perforation and retrieval considerations; magnet response differs by model. [R14] |
| Subcutaneous ICD | Subcutaneous lead and left axillary generator (80 J biphasic) | Difficult venous access | Standalone S-ICD has no chronic bradycardia or ATP function; limited post-shock pacing. Do not confuse with extravascular ICD or a combined leadless-pacing system. |

## 4.3 Pacemaker nomenclature and function (SS_CS 1.12, 1.11)

Generic pacemaker code

| **Position** | **Meaning** | **Letters** |
|---|---|---|
| I | Chamber paced | O, A, V, D |
| II | Chamber sensed | O, A, V, D |
| III | Response to sensing | O, I (inhibited), T (triggered), D (dual) |
| IV | Rate modulation | R |
| V | Multisite pacing | O, A, V, D (when specified) |

- VVI: paces and senses ventricle, inhibited by sensed beat. DDD: dual-chamber with four possible patterns (atrial and ventricular sensing = inhibition; atrial pacing and ventricular sensing; atrial sensing and ventricular pacing; atrial plus ventricular pacing). Asynchronous modes: AOO, VOO, DOO (fixed rate, no sensing).
- Bipolar leads (anode on the lead) are less susceptible to EMI than unipolar.
- Rate-responsive (R): accelerometer, minute ventilation or contractility sensors.

Programmable parameters (principles of programming, SS_CS 1.11)

- Mode and lower rate; upper tracking and sensor rates.
- Output combines amplitude (mA or V, device-specific) and pulse width (ms). For temporary pacing, measure capture threshold and apply an appropriate margin (often at least twice threshold at fixed pulse width); permanent-device safety algorithms and programming require device-team advice. [R12–R13]
- Sensitivity is a programmed mV threshold: LOWER mV means MORE sensitive. Too high a setting can miss intrinsic activity (undersensing) and permit competitive/R-on-T pacing; too low can oversense noise and inhibit pacing. Measure sensing/capture where safe; do not lower the rate or output unprotected in a dependent patient. [R13]
- AV delay (sensed and paced) and refractory periods (PVARP, blanking).
- Rate response, sleep/rest rate, magnet response, mode switch for atrial arrhythmia.
- ICD: tachycardia detection zones (rate cutoffs), anti-tachycardia pacing, shock energies (about 30–45 J delivered, charged to about 750 V), tachy therapies on/off.
- CRT: biventricular pacing, V–V timing.

Temporary-pacing troubleshooting:

- Failure to pace → check power, connections, rate/mode and oversensing.
- Failure to capture → check connection/dislodgement, output, threshold, electrolytes/ischaemia.
- Failure to sense → review lead signal and mV setting.

- Treat instability with external rescue pacing while obtaining expert help.
- Routine asynchronous backup pacing can provoke R-on-T; choose the simplest safe demand mode and recheck after clinical change. [R13]

- Preop device review: type/model, underlying rhythm and functional dependence, pacing burden, battery, thresholds, sensing, impedance trends, alerts and ICD therapy history.
  - A high pacing percentage suggests but does not prove absence of an adequate intrinsic rhythm; dependence can change under anaesthesia.
  - Historical routine follow-up intervals are ≤12 months for a simple PPM and ≤6 months for ICD/CRT; current planning may need a recent (e.g. within 3 months) interrogation/remote transmission depending on symptoms, battery, dependence and EMI risk. [R12, R14]

## 4.4 External pacemaker settings

- Apply defibrillation/pacing pads using the device’s recommended position, commonly anterior–posterior when practical. Avoid placing a pad over an implanted generator; maximise separation without delaying emergency treatment. Connect the required ECG leads for the defibrillator’s demand-pacing sensing system. [R1, R12]
- Select **demand** (sensed, inhibited) mode unless interference makes it unreliable (then fixed/asynchronous).
- Set rate (usually 60–80/min; higher rate if needed for haemodynamics).
- Increase current promptly until electrical capture, then maintain a device/protocol-appropriate safety margin above threshold (often about 10 mA). Required output varies substantially; a fixed starting/current range must not delay capture in a profoundly unstable patient. Reassess after movement and physiological change. [R1]
- Confirm **mechanical capture:** femoral/radial pulse or arterial waveform, pulse oximetry; ECG artefact can mimic capture.
- Sedation/analgesia; reassess; arrange transvenous pacing if prolonged.
- Capture often needs tens to over 100 mA and may fail despite apparent ECG capture. Treat the clinical perfusion response, confirm the monitor is not displaying pacing artefact and arrange an alternative pacing route when needed. [R1]

## 4.5 Perioperative management of CIEDs

### Preop

- Determine indication, device type (ECG, chest X-ray: ICD has thick RV shock coils), pacing dependence, last check; keep antiarrhythmics going; correct electrolytes.
- Consider reprogramming: highly dependent patient with EMI risk (asynchronous mode), switch off minute-ventilation rate response and sleep modes, switch off ICD tachy therapies immediately before surgery where EMI is likely.
- Magnets: many transvenous PPM/CRT-P devices pace asynchronously at a model/battery-dependent rate; the response may be disabled or transient.
  - ICD/CRT-D magnets usually inhibit tachycardia therapies WITHOUT making pacing asynchronous.
  - Micra leadless devices have no magnet response; AVEIR systems may respond but activation can be difficult.
  - Verify the exact device response; a pacing-dependent ICD patient with EMI risk generally needs reprogramming, not a magnet alone. [R12, R14]
- Implantable loop recorders do not deliver pacing or shocks and usually need no reprogramming. EMI can cause false recordings or overwrite clinically important data; retrieve relevant data and record procedure timing. If the surgical incision crosses the recorder site, discuss removal or relocation. [R14]

### Intraop

- Apply external defibrillation/pacing pads in advance when ICD therapies are off, pacing failure is plausible or chest access will be restricted.
  - Keep pads away from the generator (ideally >8 cm; greater separation such as 10–15 cm if feasible), but never delay a life-saving shock to achieve a distance.
  - Use standard appropriate energies. [R12]
- Monitoring: ECG showing pacing spikes (double-counting of spike and QRS possible), plethysmography, arterial line for mechanical capture; central venous access remote from leads; avoid guidewires in the heart.
- Reduce EMI: use bipolar electrosurgery where possible; if monopolar is needed, use the lowest effective power and brief bursts (generally ≤5 s) with pauses.
  - Place the dispersive electrode so current avoids the generator/leads; avoid whole-body return electrodes.
  - Risk is lower below the umbilicus when the return path is also below it and the generator is not abdominal.
  - Respond to observed inhibition immediately. [R12, R14]
- Suxamethonium: fasciculations may cause over-sensing; use with caution.
- Fixed-rate patients cannot raise heart rate for hypovolaemia: monitor output and fluid balance.
- Special procedures need a device-specific plan.
  - MRI: many MR-conditional and selected nonconditional systems can be scanned under a specialist protocol with pre/post checks, appropriate MRI mode, monitoring and rescue capability; nonconditional is not an automatic lifetime contraindication.
  - TENS is not universally prohibited, but requires interference assessment and specialist advice, particularly near the chest.
  - ECT, radiofrequency ablation, radiotherapy and lithotripsy require procedure/device-specific risk mitigation; avoid direct energy/current paths through the system rather than relying on one fixed-distance rule. [R12, R14–R15]

### Postop

- Continue ECG plus pulse/perfusion monitoring until programming/therapy status is safe. Postoperative location follows patient/procedure risk; a CIED alone does not mandate HDU. Ensure external rescue equipment remains immediately available while therapies are disabled. [R12]
- Restore settings and confirm ICD tachycardia therapies are active BEFORE leaving a monitored setting; document who checks this.
  - Interrogate after suspected malfunction, arrest/external shock, significant EMI exposure or relevant reprogramming, as agreed with the device team.
  - Uneventful temporary magnet use does not automatically require full interrogation in every case, but verify restoration and follow the planned pathway. [R12, R14]
- Watch for pocket inflammation, fever or bloodstream infection; CIED infection requires specialist assessment and frequently system extraction. Do not give extra endocarditis prophylaxis for unrelated surgery solely because a CIED is present; use standard procedure-specific prophylaxis and current infection guidance. [R10, R14]

## 4.6 Indications for external defibrillation/pacing pads before surgery (SS_CS 1.8)

- Patients with ICD or CRT-D with tachy therapies suspended.
- Pacemaker-dependent patients, or those with an unstable device where external pacing may be needed.
- High-grade block, symptomatic bradycardia or sick sinus syndrome without a temporary or permanent pacemaker.
- Consider preapplied pads for selected cardiac surgery/redo sternotomy or when access will be restricted and there is a credible pacing/defibrillation need. Epicardial wires or chest position alone do not make pads mandatory in every patient; assess the specific risk and rescue plan. [R12–R13]
- Recent unstable VT/VF, high-risk cardiomyopathy or inherited arrhythmic syndromes may justify pads and immediate rescue capability. For long QT/Brugada, review syndrome-specific triggers, electrolyte/temperature control and device plan; neither diagnosis automatically requires the same intervention for every operation. [R4, R12]
- Place pads away from the generator and choose the vector according to the defibrillator/device guidance; anterior–posterior placement is often practical. Emergency defibrillation must not be delayed for ideal positioning. [R12]

items.title: How do you read an ECG systematically?
items.q: How do you read an ECG systematically?
items.a:
- Rate, rhythm, axis.
- P waves and PR interval, QRS width and morphology.
- ST segment, T waves, QT interval.
- Compare with a previous tracing; describe findings systematically before giving a diagnosis, as emphasised in the 2010.1 WPW report.

> **Closing point:** Report what you see before you name a diagnosis.

items.title: Compare abnormal automaticity, triggered activity and re-entry as mechanisms of arrhythmia.
items.q: Compare abnormal automaticity, triggered activity and re-entry as mechanisms of arrhythmia.
items.a:
- **Abnormal automaticity** means spontaneous phase-4 depolarisation outside the sinus node; examples include ectopic atrial tachycardia, junctional tachycardia and some ventricular ectopy, often promoted by catecholamines or ischaemia.
- **Triggered activity** arises from afterdepolarisations.
  - **Early afterdepolarisations (EADs)** occur during repolarisation, classically with **long QT**, bradycardia or class Ia/III drugs, and may precipitate **torsades de pointes**.
  - **Delayed afterdepolarisations (DADs)** occur after repolarisation, classically with **digoxin toxicity**, catecholamine excess or calcium overload.
- **Re-entry** requires a circuit with two pathways of different conduction/refractory properties; examples include **AVNRT, AVRT/flutter** and many scar-related monomorphic VTs.
- Mechanism matters because treatment differs: correct triggers for automatic/triggered rhythms, but **interrupt the circuit** for re-entry (adenosine, cardioversion, ablation).

> **Closing point:** Many exam arrhythmias are re-entry, but torsades is the classic EAD rhythm.

items.title: Distinguish AF from atrial flutter on the ECG.
items.q: Distinguish AF from atrial flutter on the ECG.
items.a:
- AF: irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm without distinct P waves.
- Flutter: organised atrial activity, often near 300/min with 2:1 conduction and a ventricular rate near 150/min.
- Variable flutter block can make the ventricular rhythm irregular; AF can become regular with complete AV block/pacing.
- Inspect atrial activity and the full tracing; the 2024.2 report specifically warned against misreading AF as flutter.

> **Closing point:** An irregular rhythm requires a diagnosis from the tracing, not a slogan.

items.title: How do you approach a broad-complex tachycardia?
items.q: How do you approach a broad-complex tachycardia?
items.a:
- Treat an undifferentiated broad-complex tachycardia as VT, especially with structural disease.
- Pulseless: CPR and unsynchronised defibrillation. Unstable monomorphic VT with a pulse: synchronised cardioversion.
- Sustained polymorphic VT: unsynchronised shock even with a pulse, because synchronisation is unreliable.
- Stable monomorphic VT: expert antiarrhythmic/cardioversion plan; avoid verapamil/diltiazem for an uncertain broad rhythm.
- Pre-excited AF: cardioversion or specialist procainamide/ibutilide; avoid AV-nodal blockers including IV amiodarone.

> **Closing point:** First establish pulse, stability and monomorphic versus polymorphic rhythm.

items.title: How do you approach a regular narrow-complex tachycardia?
items.q: How do you approach a regular narrow-complex tachycardia?
items.a:
- Check stability and whether this is re-entry, flutter, atrial tachycardia or sinus tachycardia from a cause.
- Unstable re-entry/flutter: synchronised cardioversion; treat causes of sinus tachycardia.
- Stable re-entry: suitable vagal manoeuvre, then adenosine 6 mg rapid IV/flush, followed by 12 mg; further dosing per protocol.
- Selected beta-blocker or verapamil/diltiazem if BP and ventricular function permit. Adenosine can treat regular narrow orthodromic AVRT in WPW; avoid it in pre-excited AF.

> **Closing point:** Adenosine terminates AV-node-dependent re-entry; flutter may only be unmasked.

items.title: What are the adverse features that make a tachycardia unstable?
items.q: What are the adverse features that make a tachycardia unstable?
items.a:
- Shock/hypotension, syncope or reduced consciousness.
- Myocardial ischaemia or acute heart failure.
- Decide whether the arrhythmia is causing the instability while treating triggers in parallel.
- Synchronise for unstable AF/flutter/regular monomorphic tachycardia; use an unsynchronised shock for sustained polymorphic VT or VF/pulseless VT.

> **Closing point:** Instability requires prompt rhythm-appropriate treatment.

items.title: Which electrolyte disturbances provoke arrhythmias, and what are the targets?
items.q: Which electrolyte disturbances provoke arrhythmias, and what are the targets?
items.a:
- Hypo- and hyperkalaemia can cause serious arrhythmia; low Mg/Ca may prolong repolarisation.
- Correct deficiencies, monitor ECG/levels and account for renal function and ongoing losses.
- Selected TdP/long-QT patients may need high-normal potassium; K ≥4.5 and Mg ≥1 mmol/L are not universal targets for every tachyarrhythmia.
- Hyperkalaemic ECG changes are variable; a normal ECG does not exclude dangerous hyperkalaemia.

> **Closing point:** Correct the abnormality without causing a new one.

items.title: Why does laparoscopy cause arrhythmias?
items.q: Why does laparoscopy cause arrhythmias?
items.a:
- Peritoneal stretch can trigger vagal bradycardia/asystole; stop the stimulus and release insufflation if severe.
- CO2 absorption/hypoventilation, hypoxaemia and sympathetic stimulation can provoke tachyarrhythmia.
- Pneumoperitoneum increases afterload and may reduce venous return; tilt and volume status modify the effect.
- Support airway/perfusion, treat the rhythm (adult ANZCOR atropine 500–600 micrograms for appropriate bradycardia) and exclude bleeding, gas embolism or ischaemia.

> **Closing point:** Treat the stimulus, rhythm and cause together.

items.title: What are the causes of new perioperative atrial fibrillation?
items.q: What are the causes of new perioperative atrial fibrillation?
items.a:
- Sepsis, hypovolaemia, pain and catecholamines.
- Electrolytes, hypoxia, PE and ischaemia.
- Thyroid disease and drug withdrawal (beta-blockers).
- Cardiac and thoracic surgery are high risk.

> **Closing point:** AF is usually a sign, not a diagnosis.

items.title: What is CHA2DS2-VASc?
items.q: What is CHA2DS2-VASc?
items.a:
- CHA2DS2-VASc: heart failure, hypertension, age ≥75 (2), diabetes, prior stroke/TIA/embolism (2), vascular disease, age 65–74 and female sex as a modifier.
- ESC 2024 uses **CHA2DS2-VA**, removing sex: consider OAC at 1 and recommend at ≥2, unless contraindicated.
- Other guidelines retain CHA2DS2-VASc/estimated annual risk; use the locally adopted method and clinical judgement.
- Bleeding assessment guides correction and shared decisions; sinus rhythm after cardioversion/ablation does not erase stroke risk.

> **Closing point:** Know the score and which guideline uses it.

items.title: When can AF be cardioverted without anticoagulation?
items.q: When can AF be cardioverted without anticoagulation?
items.a:
- Haemodynamic emergency: cardiovert promptly; do not delay for TOE or anticoagulation, then anticoagulate when appropriate.
- For non-emergency AF >24 h or unknown duration, ESC 2024 advises ≥3 weeks therapeutic OAC or TOE to exclude thrombus.
- Generally continue OAC for ≥4 weeks after cardioversion; narrow low-risk exceptions need an explicit guideline-based decision.
- Long-term OAC depends on thromboembolic risk; “under 48 hours” is not blanket protection.

> **Closing point:** A clear TOE does not remove post-cardioversion embolic risk.

items.title: What is the ALS algorithm for VF or pulseless VT?
items.q: What is the ALS algorithm for VF or pulseless VT?
items.a:
- CPR 30:2 and defibrillation as soon as possible.
- Shock, 2 minutes of CPR, then reassess.
- Adrenaline 1 mg after the second shock, then every 3 to 5 minutes.
- Amiodarone 300 mg after the third shock, 150 mg after the fifth.
- Treat 4Hs and 4Ts.

> **Closing point:** Early defibrillation is the most important step.

items.title: What is torsades de pointes and how is it treated?
items.q: What is torsades de pointes and how is it treated?
items.a:
- Polymorphic VT associated with prolonged QT; may self-terminate or become sustained/VF.
- Sustained polymorphic VT: unsynchronised shock even with a pulse; CPR if pulseless. Do not delay shock for magnesium.
- Stop QT drugs and correct causes; IV magnesium even with normal Mg. ANZCOR 11.9 specifies 5 mmol over 10 min, repeat once if needed; other protocols use MgSO4 2 g (~8 mmol)—follow the selected protocol/urgency.
- Expert overdrive pacing for recurrence; isoprenaline only for selected acquired pause-dependent TdP, not routine congenital LQTS. Avoid amiodarone.

> **Closing point:** Shock sustained polymorphic VT; magnesium helps prevent recurrence.

items.title: Outline the Vaughan Williams classification.
items.q: Outline the Vaughan Williams classification.
items.a:
- I: sodium channel blockers (a, b, c).
- II: beta-blockers.
- III: potassium channel blockers (amiodarone, sotalol).
- IV: calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem).
- Others: adenosine, digoxin, magnesium.

> **Closing point:** Remember it by the channel blocked.

items.title: What are the anaesthetic issues with amiodarone?
items.q: What are the anaesthetic issues with amiodarone?
items.a:
- Long half-life, so effects persist for weeks.
- Bradycardia and hypotension at induction, which may be resistant to atropine.
- QT prolongation; thyroid, lung and liver toxicity.
- Continue perioperatively; IV causes phlebitis and hypotension.

> **Closing point:** Expect a slow heart rate and vasodilation.

items.title: How is adenosine given and what are its pitfalls?
items.q: How is adenosine given and what are its pitfalls?
items.a:
- 6 mg rapid IV into a suitable large vein with flush, then 12 mg; repeat 12 mg if needed under ANZCOR.
- Transient asystole, bronchospasm, chest tightness.
- Reduce the initial dose for central administration/transplanted hearts according to protocol; methylxanthines can antagonise the effect.
- Potentiated by dipyridamole.

> **Closing point:** Warn the patient and have pads attached.

items.title: What are the features of digoxin toxicity and how is it treated?
items.q: What are the features of digoxin toxicity and how is it treated?
items.a:
- GI symptoms, visual changes, bradycardia/block, atrial tachycardia with block or ventricular/bidirectional VT.
- Renal impairment and low K/Mg increase toxicity; severe acute poisoning may instead cause hyperkalaemia.
- Stop digoxin, check ECG/electrolytes/renal function and timed level; use digoxin-specific Fab for life-threatening toxicity.
- Seek toxicology advice; avoid elective cardioversion, but do not withhold a lifesaving shock. Pacing may be proarrhythmic and needs expert use.

> **Closing point:** Fab treats severe toxicity; correct the physiological consequences as well.

items.title: Why should you avoid AV nodal blockers in pre-excited AF?
items.q: Why should you avoid AV nodal blockers in pre-excited AF?
items.a:
- AV-nodal blockade can favour very rapid accessory-pathway conduction and trigger VF.
- Avoid adenosine, digoxin, beta-blockers, verapamil/diltiazem **and IV amiodarone** in pre-excited AF.
- Unstable: synchronised cardioversion if feasible; stable: expert procainamide/ibutilide or electrical cardioversion.
- Regular narrow orthodromic AVRT is different and can appropriately respond to adenosine.

> **Closing point:** Identify the rhythm before choosing an AV-nodal drug.

items.title: What are the energy requirements and technique for synchronised cardioversion?
items.q: What are the energy requirements and technique for synchronised cardioversion?
items.a:
- Check R-wave synchronisation markers before every shock; many devices reset sync after a shock.
- Use device/rhythm-appropriate energy: AF often starts at 200 J biphasic; flutter/regular SVT often 50–100 J; monomorphic VT often 100–150 J. Follow the validated local/device protocol.
- AP or anterolateral pads, good contact and escalation after failure; keep pads away from CIED generators where practical.
- Brief titrated anaesthesia/sedation with oxygen, airway support and monitoring; do not delay an emergency shock. Sustained polymorphic VT is shocked unsynchronised.

> **Closing point:** Check sync and the rhythm, not just the joules.

items.title: Biphasic versus monophasic defibrillators: what is the difference?
items.q: Biphasic versus monophasic defibrillators: what is the difference?
items.a:
- Monophasic current flows one way; biphasic reverses direction during the shock.
- Biphasic waveforms achieve defibrillation at lower nominal energy, but setting depends on the device; monophasic adult defibrillation uses 360 J.
- Many biphasic devices adjust waveform for impedance; effective current also depends on pad contact and patient factors.
- Joules measure energy; amperes measure current. Lower energy is not a guarantee of less clinical myocardial injury in every comparison.

> **Closing point:** Use the manufacturer’s validated waveform and energy settings.

items.title: What are the hazards of defibrillation?
items.q: What are the hazards of defibrillation?
items.a:
- Failure to shock, VF/asystole, burns, myocardial injury.
- Shock to staff; fire in an oxygen-rich environment.
- Pacemaker or ICD damage.
- Thromboembolism after cardioversion.

> **Closing point:** Clear the patient and oxygen before the shock.

items.title: What is the role of flecainide and why is it dangerous after infarction?
items.q: What is the role of flecainide and why is it dangerous after infarction?
items.a:
- Class Ic sodium-channel blockade slows conduction and can depress contractility/widen QRS.
- Used for selected AF/SVT with no significant structural/ischaemic heart disease; specialist AV-nodal co-treatment may prevent 1:1 flutter.
- CAST found excess arrhythmic mortality with encainide/flecainide after MI; this does not prove every class I drug is harmful in every patient.
- Toxicity: resuscitation, toxicology advice and sodium bicarbonate for sodium-channel blockade.

> **Closing point:** Avoid flecainide in significant structural/ischaemic heart disease.

items.title: Classify AV block and name the high-risk forms.
items.q: Classify AV block and name the high-risk forms.
items.a:
- First-degree: PR >200 ms with all P waves conducted.
- Mobitz I: progressive PR prolongation then a dropped QRS; Mobitz II: intermittent nonconducted P with otherwise fixed PR.
- A 2:1 block cannot reliably be labelled Mobitz I versus II from the ratio alone; third-degree block has complete AV dissociation.
- Acquired Mobitz II, high-grade or complete AV block without a reversible cause warrants permanent-pacing assessment regardless of symptoms.

> **Closing point:** High-grade infranodal block needs a pacing plan.

items.title: What is trifascicular block and does it need a pacemaker?
items.q: What is trifascicular block and does it need a pacemaker?
items.a:
- The traditional label often means bifascicular block plus PR prolongation.
- PR prolongation may be AV-nodal, so this ECG does not prove disease in all three fascicles.
- Stable asymptomatic bifascicular block plus long PR does not automatically need prophylactic temporary pacing.
- Syncope, alternating BBB or documented advanced AV block requires cardiology/pacing assessment.

> **Closing point:** Alternating BBB is a different risk from an isolated long PR.

items.title: When is preoperative pacing indicated?
items.q: When is preoperative pacing indicated?
items.a:
- Acquired Mobitz II, high-grade or complete AV block not due to a reversible cause: permanent-pacing assessment even without symptoms.
- Alternating bundle-branch block and selected symptomatic conduction disease.
- Symptomatic sinus-node dysfunction when symptoms correlate; treat reversible causes first.
- Urgent unstable bradycardia may need temporary pacing while arranging definitive treatment; asymptomatic bifascicular block alone is not an indication.

> **Closing point:** Pacing indication depends on the conduction diagnosis, not symptoms alone.

items.title: What are the types of temporary pacing?
items.q: What are the types of temporary pacing?
items.a:
- Transcutaneous: rapid external rescue, confirm mechanical capture.
- Transvenous: ventricular endocardial lead, useful when prolonged reliable temporary support is required.
- Epicardial: wires placed at cardiac surgery.
- Transoesophageal: mainly atrial stimulation; not reliable ventricular rescue for complete AV block.

> **Closing point:** Choose a method capable of capturing the chamber that needs support.

items.title: How do you perform transcutaneous pacing?
items.q: How do you perform transcutaneous pacing?
items.a:
- Pads anterior-posterior, ECG leads connected.
- Set rate 70 to 80/min, increase current until capture.
- Confirm mechanical capture with a pulse or arterial line.
- Sedation and analgesia in the awake patient.

> **Closing point:** Electrical capture is not mechanical capture.

items.title: What are the settings on an external pacemaker?
items.q: What are the settings on an external pacemaker?
items.a:
- Mode: VVI, DDD or AAI according to rhythm, wires and AV conduction; avoid AAI for complete AV block. Use the monitor’s pacing-detection mode where available.
- Rate and output (mA), then confirm electrical and mechanical capture.
- Sensitivity (mV): a lower number is more sensitive; set with a measured safety margin when safe.
- Dual-chamber AV delay and atrial/ventricular settings; threshold checks need trained staff and backup if dependent.

> **Closing point:** A capture margin matters, but never test dependence without protection.

items.title: Explain failure to capture and its causes.
items.q: Explain failure to capture and its causes.
items.a:
- Pacing spikes without a QRS.
- Increase output; check connections and polarity.
- Threshold rises with electrolyte, drug, ischaemia and fibrosis effects.
- Wire displacement; use another wire or pads.

> **Closing point:** Increase output first, then check connections.

items.title: What is the effect of over-sensing and under-sensing?
items.q: What is the effect of over-sensing and under-sensing?
items.a:
- Over-sensing: pacing inhibited, pauses (EMI, myopotentials).
- Under-sensing: pacing spikes at the wrong time, competitive pacing and R-on-T.
- Adjust the sensitivity: lower mV means more sensitive.
- Treat the interference source.

> **Closing point:** Over-sensing causes pauses; under-sensing causes extra spikes.

items.title: What is the NBG pacemaker code?
items.q: What is the NBG pacemaker code?
items.a:
- I: chamber paced; II: chamber sensed (O, A, V, D).
- III: response (O, I, T, D).
- IV: rate modulation (R).
- V: multisite pacing.

> **Closing point:** First three letters are most important.

items.title: What does DDD pacing do?
items.q: What does DDD pacing do?
items.a:
- Paces and senses both chambers.
- Responds by inhibition or triggering.
- Tracks atrial rate to maintain AV synchrony.
- Limited by an upper tracking rate.

> **Closing point:** Preserves AV synchrony.

items.title: What is pacemaker syndrome, why does it occur and how is it managed?
items.q: What is pacemaker syndrome, why does it occur and how is it managed?
items.a:
